entities.name: Adalberon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adalberon of Reims (c. 920–989) was Archbishop of Reims and one of the most politically powerful churchmen of tenth-century France. Chancellor of the Carolingian kings Lothair and Louis V, he eventually played a decisive role in the political crisis that ended Carolingian rule and established the Capetian dynasty. His career exemplified the archbishop of Reims's unique position as both a spiritual leader and a kingmaker in French history.

Reims was the coronation city of French kings, and its archbishop's endorsement was critical to royal legitimacy. Adalberon's complex political allegiances — nominally Carolingian chancellor but ultimately engineering the succession of Hugh Capet — have made him one of the most controversial figures in French medieval historiography. His shift to Hugh Capet's cause in 987 has been interpreted variously as political pragmatism, pro-imperial inclination, or principled rejection of a weak Carolingian claimant.

At the synod of Senlis in 987 — the key election assembly — Adalberon delivered the speech that effectively declared Hugh Capet's election, crowning him king in July 987. This moment ended 241 years of Carolingian rule and began the Capetian dynasty that would last 987–1328 and shape France as a state. Adalberon's role at this hinge of French history makes him one of the most consequential archbishops in French history, regardless of his personal motivations.
